html:
Sarai was the capital of the Golden Horde, the western khanate of the Mongol Empire, on the lower Volga in what is now southern Russia. Batu Khan founded it around 1250, after the Mongol conquest of the Russian lands, and it grew into one of the largest cities of the medieval world.

It stood where the river trade from the north met the caravan routes from Central Asia and the Black Sea, so furs, slaves, silk and spices passed through. Ibn Battuta, who came in the 1330s, described a big crowded city of many peoples, Mongols, Kipchaks, Russians, Alans, Greeks and Italian merchants, with many mosques. Russian princes travelled here to receive their patents to rule.

There were probably two Sarais: the first, Sarai Batu, and a later New Sarai, or Sarai Berke, upriver, which became the capital under Özbeg Khan, who made Islam the state faith. Scholars still argue over which ruins are which. Timur sacked Sarai in 1395. Plague and civil war had already weakened it, and it never recovered.
